Description: 日常叙事 · 一把借来的旧雨伞
DescriptionEn: Choose a short excerpt or read and type the complete text
LongText: The rain began while I was choosing apples. By the time I reached the shop door, the pavement had become a shallow stream. The woman behind the counter handed me a blue umbrella with a wooden handle. She did not ask for my name or a deposit. She only asked me to bring it back before Thursday, when her father would need it for his walk to the market. On the way home, I noticed a repair near the edge. Someone had stitched the fabric with yellow thread, making a little sun in the middle of all that blue. The umbrella leaned to one side, so I had to turn it whenever the wind changed. It was more work than using my own, which was waiting, perfectly dry and completely useless, in a cupboard at home. I returned on Wednesday with the umbrella and a paper bag of pears. The woman was arranging jars on a high shelf. Her father sat by the window, reading the weather forecast as if he could negotiate with it. He thanked me for the pears but said the umbrella had already earned its keep. Apparently, it had sheltered half the street over the years, including a musician, two delivery riders, and a bride whose car had broken down. Before I left, he showed me a small label beneath the handle. It carried the shop's address in fading ink. No telephone number, no warning about loss, just a place to return to. That evening I finally moved my own umbrella out of the cupboard. I put it beside the front door, where I might actually remember it. Then I found a strip of yellow ribbon and tied it around the handle, partly so I could recognise it, and partly because I liked the thought of carrying a small bright thing into the next rainy day.

She only asked me to bring it back before Thursday, when her father would need it for his walk to the market.
Title: The borrowed umbrella

Description: 旅行观察 · 车窗与一张手绘地图
DescriptionEn: Choose a short excerpt or read and type the complete text
LongText: I booked a window seat for the early train, hoping to watch the coast appear after the city ended. Instead, the glass reflected a man eating toast, a sleeping child, and my own face above a paper cup. For the first twenty minutes, the world outside was only a series of walls. Then the train crossed a bridge, the buildings fell away, and a strip of water caught the morning light. Across the aisle, a boy was drawing a map on the back of an envelope. He asked his mother whether the sea belonged on the left or the right. She said it depended on which way he was facing. He considered this an unreasonable complication and drew water on both sides. His map also included a large bakery, although we had not passed one. It was the place he hoped to visit when they arrived. I had brought a difficult book and a list of messages to answer. Both remained in my bag. There were small stations with empty benches, gardens divided by hedges, and a dog that ran beside the train for three enthusiastic seconds. At one platform, a woman held a bunch of flowers upside down while searching for her ticket. A conductor waited without looking annoyed. The delay lasted less than a minute, but it was enough for the boy to add a flower shop to his map. Near our destination, the train slowed beside a row of boats resting on mud. The tide was out, and the harbour looked unfinished. I had expected a blue postcard view; what I got was a working place between two busy parts of its day. The boy folded his map and checked that the bakery was still visible. When we stepped onto the platform, he turned in a complete circle to find the correct direction. I let my messages wait a little longer and followed the smell of warm bread towards the station doors.

Then the train crossed a bridge, the buildings fell away, and a strip of water caught the morning light.

Description: 厨房随笔 · 从一张收据开始的食谱
DescriptionEn: Choose a short excerpt or read and type the complete text
LongText: My brother wrote the soup recipe on a receipt because we could not find any paper. He listed carrots, onions, beans, and a quantity of water described only as enough. When I called to ask what that meant, he told me to look in the pot. This was not helpful advice for someone who had already used a pot that was too small and spilled half the onions onto the floor. The first batch tasted mainly of pepper. The second was better, although the beans remained firm long after everything else had softened. I bought a notebook and began recording what actually happened: how long the onions needed, which beans came from a tin, and whether the lid had stayed on. I also noted things that had nothing to do with cooking. There was a delivery at half past six. It rained. My neighbour knocked to borrow a chair. After a few weeks, the recipe occupied three pages. The soup itself had changed. I used a little lemon at the end and left out an expensive herb that seemed to disappear without contributing anything. On cold evenings, I toasted bread while the pot simmered. On warmer ones, I opened the kitchen window and heard the people downstairs arguing cheerfully about their garden. Cooking stopped feeling like an examination in which I had missed the instructions. When my brother visited, he asked where I had found the recipe. I showed him the receipt, now tucked into the notebook, with a grease mark covering the price of a bus ticket. He laughed at all my careful measurements, then asked whether he could photograph the page about the beans. We ate at the small kitchen table with the borrowed chair between us. There was enough soup for another meal, which turned out to be the most useful measurement of all. Before washing the pot, I wrote one final note: this amount feeds two people now and one person tomorrow.

Description: 城市生活 · 找得到的修理铺
DescriptionEn: Choose a short excerpt or read and type the complete text
LongText: The library noticeboard had a map of places that could repair things. A red pin marked a bicycle workshop, a green one marked a tailor, and a blue one marked a man who fixed lamps from his garage. I had come to return a book, but I stayed to copy an address. My desk lamp had been dark for months, and I had almost forgotten that it could be anything else. The garage was behind a house with three different doorbells. A handwritten sign told visitors to use the smallest one. Inside, shelves held wires, switches, and glass shades wrapped in newspaper. The man examined my lamp beneath another lamp that looked much older. He asked whether I wanted a new switch or a switch that matched the original. I had never imagined that this would be a decision I needed to make. While he worked, I looked at a radio on the bench. Its owner had attached a note explaining that the evening news sounded too quiet but the weather report sounded normal. The man said such descriptions were often more useful than technical guesses. People knew how their belongings behaved, even when they did not know the names of the parts inside. He tested a connection, moved a wire, and my lamp lit up with an ordinary yellow glow. On the walk home, I passed two of the other places from the map. The tailor's window displayed a coat with bright new buttons. Outside the bicycle workshop, someone was adjusting a saddle for a child who could barely stand still. I thought about how many useful doors I had walked past without knowing what happened behind them. Back at my desk, the lamp illuminated the book I had forgotten to return. I placed the library receipt beside it and added a reminder for Saturday. This time, I would bring a spare pin for the noticeboard and the address of the garage, written clearly enough for the next person.

Description: 街区故事 · 放映开始前的一块蛋糕
DescriptionEn: Choose a short excerpt or read and type the complete text
LongText: The smallest cinema in town had only six rows of seats. I usually chose the last one because the radiator made a clicking noise near the front. On Friday, an elderly couple arrived carrying a cake in a square tin. The ticket seller brought them two plates and a pair of forks. Nobody explained the arrangement, and nobody seemed surprised, so I assumed I was the only person who had missed a tradition. Before the film, the projector stopped. A pale rectangle hung on the screen while someone upstairs moved equipment with the careful noises of a person trying not to sound worried. The audience waited. A woman checked the time, and a man offered a completely impractical suggestion about replacing a cable. Then the couple opened their tin. It was a birthday cake, they said, and it would be easier to share while the lights were still on. Paper plates appeared from behind the ticket desk. There were enough slices for everyone, although some had to use teaspoons. I learned that the couple had watched their first film together in that room forty years earlier. Neither remembered the title. They disagreed about whether it had rained that night, and whether the building had already smelled of warm dust. The ticket seller said it had probably smelled that way since the day it opened. The projector started just as I finished my slice. Everyone clapped, partly for the technician and partly because we had become a small audience with something to clap about. The film was a quiet story about two sisters clearing out a house. I liked it, but afterwards I found myself remembering the interval that had happened before the beginning. When I returned the following week, the radiator still clicked, and I still chose the last row. There was no cake. The ticket seller recognised me, though, and asked whether I had enjoyed Friday. I said yes before remembering that she might have meant the film.

On Friday, an elderly couple arrived carrying a cake in a square tin. The ticket seller brought them two plates and a pair of forks. Nobody explained the arrangement, and nobody seemed surprised, so I assumed I was the only person who had missed a tradition.

Description: 生活观察 · 清晨面馆里的人和声音
DescriptionEn: Choose a short excerpt or read and type the complete text
LongText: 下夜班时，街上的早餐摊刚亮灯。我走进巷口的面馆，老板没有问，先把电风扇转向里面。靠窗的桌子还湿着，纸巾盒上压着一张今天的报纸。我点了小碗面，坐下来才发现，口袋里那支工作时一直找不到的笔，原来别在外套领子上，笔帽已经被我按松了。 老板在柜台后包馄饨，动作不快，托盘里却很快排出整齐的几行。他问我要不要葱，我说少一点。等面端上来，葱花单独装在小碟里，旁边还放了半个卤蛋。我正要说自己没点，他指了指门口的牌子，原来早上七点以前，小碗面也送半个蛋。 隔壁桌坐着一个送货的人，头盔搁在膝上，手机响了两回，他都没有接。第三回响的时候，他先把嘴里的面咽下去，才很轻地说，已经到了，马上进门。我以为他会立刻离开，他却继续喝汤。过了几分钟，一个背书包的小女孩跑进来，把自己的豆浆放在他面前，拿走了桌上的包子。 天渐渐亮了，玻璃上能看清对面药店的招牌。老板去门外挪开挡路的空箱子，回来时顺手带进一把折叠椅，说今天有学生来得早，里面可能坐不下。我想起小时候上学，总觉得早餐店的人从来不睡觉。如今坐在这里，才看见他们也会揉眼睛，也会把刚沏的茶放凉了忘记喝。 结账时，我把那支笔留在柜台上，提醒老板记得拧紧笔帽。他说找零的小本子正缺一支。我出门走了几步，听见他在后面喊，以后下班晚，灯亮着就进来。巷子另一头的公交车刚好靠站，我没有赶，慢慢走回住处，鞋底踩过树影，肚子里还留着一点热汤。

Description: 阅读随笔 · 一本旧书夹着的小城记忆
DescriptionEn: Choose a short excerpt or read and type the complete text
LongText: 旧书店搬进了楼上的小房间，楼梯比我记得的窄。老板把推理小说放在门边，说这样等人时也能翻两页。我挑了一本旅行随笔，书里掉出一张褪色的车票，终点站是我小时候住过的小城。票根上的日期看不清，只剩售票员用铅笔画的一道斜线，压在纸纹里。 我问这张车票是不是也卖。老板正在修一个松动的书架，听完笑了，说夹在书里的东西，如果没有失主来找，就跟书一起走。柜台后有一只饼干盒，里面放着不能随便带走的照片和信。他每隔一段时间会拍照发出去，有时真能等到人回来认领，但更多时候，盒子只是越来越满。 那本随笔写得很慢，有整整一页都在讲旅馆窗外的一棵树。我原本只想看看目录，却站着读了十多分钟。窗边有人轻声背单词，念错了便从头再来。楼下修鞋的机器隔一会儿响一下，像在替他划分段落。我忽然觉得，书店搬到这里，反而比原来临街时更容易让人待住。 付款时，老板给我找了一个旧信封装书，免得外面的毛毛雨打湿封面。他看了一眼车票，问那座小城有什么好吃的。我说车站旁边以前有家卖烧饼的铺子，出炉时会在门口放一只竹篮，但我已经好多年没回去，不知道还在不在。他说，下次查到了，可以在书页上夹一张新的便签。 回家后，我没有把车票贴进收藏册，只让它留在原来的章节。那一页讲的是作者临时改签，错过末班车，最后在陌生车站等到清晨。我读完，把书放在床头，才去查回小城的时刻表。屏幕上的车次多了很多，地名却还是熟悉的两个字。厨房水烧开时，我暂时关掉网页，想着先把这本书读完再说。

Description: 街边记事 · 河岸上的一个冬日早晨
DescriptionEn: Choose a short excerpt or read and type the complete text
LongText: 降温以后，小河边的人少了。常来钓鱼的大叔把凳子搬到桥洞下，保温杯换成了更大的一只。我沿着步道去买菜，看见芦苇里挂着一只红色气球，已经瘪了一半，风吹过时，它还是努力往上抬。我停下来辨认拴气球的线，才发现线头缠在一截枯枝上，离岸边并不远。 钓鱼的大叔看见我张望，问是不是丢了东西。我指给他看，他从包里拿出一根能伸长的抄网杆，试了两下，把枯枝和气球一起拖过来。气球上印着一只戴帽子的熊，背面有人写了生日快乐。字被水洇开了，只有最后一个感叹号还十分清楚。他说今天鱼没钓到，倒是先捞到一个句号，我提醒他那是感叹号，他便认真看了一眼。 我们把线解下来，分开放进垃圾桶。桥上的自行车一辆接一辆过去，轮胎压过接缝，发出短短的两声。过去我总觉得这条河没什么可看，夏天蚊子多，冬天水又浅。那天站在桥下，才留意到石阶旁有几枚鸟脚印，岸边的草虽然黄了，根部却露着很细的新叶。 买完菜回来，大叔换了一个位置，正耐心地替另一个人解鱼线。两副线团缠在一起，很难分清哪段属于谁。他们没有急，先把各自的鱼竿平放好，再一点点往外抽。河面上有一小片阳光，随着桥影慢慢移动。我走得比去时更慢，塑料袋里的萝卜叶偶尔碰到裤脚，凉凉的。 后来连着几天下雨，我从公交车窗里经过小河，只看见桥洞下空着的那块地方。周末放晴，再去买菜时，熟悉的凳子又摆回来了。大叔朝我点了点头，举起杯子，像是说明今天的水还热着。我没有过去打扰，只沿着河岸继续走，顺手把挂在栏杆上的一条废鱼线收进了袋子。

Description: 居家随笔 · 整理纸箱时认识的新邻居
DescriptionEn: Choose a short excerpt or read and type the complete text
LongText: 搬家后的第三天，客厅还剩最后一个纸箱。箱子上写着杂物，字是我自己写的，却想不起里面装了什么。我绕着它走了好几回，直到外卖放上去，才发现这个高度正好能当临时小桌。那晚我坐在地板上吃饭，窗外有人练笛子，总在同一个地方停下来，再从上一句重新吹。 周六上午，我终于划开胶带。最上面是两条不同颜色的充电线、一只空相框和几本说明书。再往下，是以前房东留下的备用钥匙，已经不该继续带着了。我把它放进信封，准备下周经过老房子时送回去。箱底还压着一把小尺子，边角有咬过的痕迹，大概是很早以前养猫时留下的。 我本想把东西分成留下和扔掉两堆，结果地板上很快出现第三堆：需要想一想。相框的背板坏了，但可以修；说明书对应的电器早已送人，可其中夹着保修时写下的电话号码。新家阳光很好，一下午都照在这些不起眼的小东西上，把灰尘和划痕照得格外清楚，也让我没有办法随手把它们重新塞回箱子。 傍晚，楼下邻居来借螺丝刀。他在门口看见拆开的相框，说自己正好多买了一块薄木板，能替我裁一块合适的背板。我们此前只在电梯里见过，彼此甚至不知道姓什么。等他量好尺寸，我才想起来问。他说姓许，言午许，我便在手机上记下，旁边加了相框两个字，怕以后又对不上人。 纸箱清空以后，我把它折平，靠在门后，等收废品的人来。原来放箱子的地方空出一块地板，房间显得大了一点，也安静了一点。第二天许叔送来背板，我从抽屉里找出一张旧照片，装进去放在窗台。笛声又从楼下传上来，这回顺利吹过了那句。我正给植物浇水，手停了停，听他把后面的一小段也吹完了。

Description: 街角故事 · 一次很普通的补胎
DescriptionEn: Choose a short excerpt or read and type the complete text
LongText: 自行车的后轮总是慢慢漏气，打满以后能骑两天，第三天推起来就费劲。我把车送到街角，修车师傅先让我去旁边坐着。他没急着拆轮胎，而是转了转气门，往上抹了一点肥皂水。几颗小泡泡挤在一起，他抬头说，找到地方了，今天不用把整个轮子卸下来，你等一会儿就好。 摊子搭在一棵梧桐树下，工具挂在旧木板上，每件都有固定的位置。一只橘猫趴在打气筒旁，别人经过它不动，师傅伸手拿扳手时，它才慢吞吞地换个方向。我问是不是他养的，他说只是一起上班，工资由附近几家轮流发，有时是鱼，有时是半罐猫粮，待遇比修车的人还稳定。 隔壁卖水果的大姐搬来一张凳子，问能不能替她拧紧螺丝。师傅指指手边的车，让她先把凳子留着。大姐顺便放下两个橘子，说今年这批有点酸，别一口吃太大。他擦干净手，剥开一个，分了一半给我。果然酸得很直接，我们都没有立刻说话，只看着街对面的公交站，等那股酸味慢慢过去。 轮胎修好以后，师傅又捏了捏刹车，替我把松掉的车灯抬高一点。他说天黑得早，别只顾着看路面，也让对面的人看见你。我试骑了一小段，后轮不再发软，车铃却响得不太利索。刚要回来请他再看，他已经在修那张凳子。我想了想，决定下回再说，这样至少又有一个理由过来坐几分钟。 回家的路并不远，我特意绕到河边，让刚充足气的轮子多转一会儿。经过缓坡时，不用像前几天那样站起来使劲踩。车篮里放着师傅硬塞给我的另一个橘子，他说酸的东西留到饭后吃，也许就没有那么酸。我把车停在楼下，按了两次不太清脆的铃，抬头看见自家的窗户还亮着，才锁好车，慢慢走上楼。

Description: 自拟议论文题 · 公共图书馆应优先投入数字服务还是实体空间，讨论双方并给出观点 · 短篇为节选，长篇为完整原创回答
DescriptionEn: Original prompt: should public libraries prioritise digital services or physical space? Discuss both views and give your opinion
LongText: Some people argue that public libraries should spend most of their money on digital services, while others believe that physical buildings remain their main responsibility. In my view, libraries need reliable online access, but reducing the building to a minor part of their work would exclude many of the people who depend on them. Digital services have clear advantages. A reader who works irregular hours can borrow an electronic book without travelling across town before closing time. Online catalogues also make collections easier to search, and digital materials can be particularly useful for people who need larger text. These benefits justify substantial investment. A library with an attractive building but an unreliable website may be difficult to use for residents who cannot visit regularly. However, a physical library provides more than storage for books. Students may need a quiet desk because their homes are crowded. Older residents may need a member of staff to explain an unfamiliar form, rather than a link to another page. Even access to digital resources sometimes depends on the building: a person without a suitable device or stable internet connection cannot benefit fully from an expanded online collection. Closing study areas to fund more electronic subscriptions could therefore undermine the purpose of that spending. Budgets should reflect local needs rather than a fixed preference for one format. In a district where most residents have internet access but the library building is unsafe, repairs should come first. Elsewhere, extending remote access might help more people than adding another room. Libraries can gather evidence through usage records and conversations with residents, including those who rarely visit. I would therefore support a balanced approach, with a protected budget for accessible buildings and targeted improvements to digital services. The useful question is which barrier a particular investment removes. Neither a shelf of books nor an online collection is sufficient if the people who need it cannot actually use it.
ShortText: Some people argue that public libraries should spend most of their money on digital services, while others believe that physical buildings remain their main responsibility. In my view, libraries need reliable online access, but reducing the building to a minor part of their work would exclude many of the people who depend on them.

Description: 自拟议论文题 · 中学应否用实践小组项目替代部分备考时间，说明同意程度并举例 · 短篇为节选，长篇为完整原创回答
DescriptionEn: Original prompt: should secondary schools replace some exam preparation with practical group projects? Explain how far you agree
LongText: It is sometimes suggested that secondary schools should replace part of their examination preparation with practical group projects. I largely agree, provided that projects have clear learning goals and do not remove the individual assessment that students still need. A carefully planned project can reveal whether students are able to use knowledge beyond a familiar question on a test. One benefit is that practical work connects subjects that are often taught separately. For example, students investigating food waste in their cafeteria could measure quantities, calculate costs, interview staff, and write a proposal. The mathematics would have a visible purpose, while the report would require accurate evidence rather than attractive language alone. Such work also gives teachers opportunities to notice misunderstandings during the process, instead of discovering them only when an examination has finished. Group projects can also teach students how to divide responsibilities and deal with disagreement. These skills are difficult to practise through silent revision. However, simply placing four students around a table does not guarantee cooperation. One confident student may take over, while another contributes little. Teachers should therefore require short individual records and speak to each student about the group's decisions. Assessment should recognise both the shared result and each person's understanding. There are limits to how much examination preparation should be replaced. Students still need time to develop fluency in basic procedures and to practise working independently. Projects also require materials, planning, and feedback, which may put additional pressure on schools with limited resources. Starting with one modest project each term would be more realistic than redesigning every subject at once. Overall, I support replacing some repetitive test practice with well supervised projects. The aim should be to add opportunities to apply knowledge, while keeping sufficient individual work to show what each student has learned. With that balance, practical projects can strengthen academic learning rather than compete with it.
ShortText: It is sometimes suggested that secondary schools should replace part of their examination preparation with practical group projects. I largely agree, provided that projects have clear learning goals and do not remove the individual assessment that students still need. A carefully planned project can reveal whether students are able to use knowledge beyond a familiar question on a test.

DescriptionEn: Original prompt: fund a film night or a repair workshop? Maya favours broad participation; Daniel raises safety concerns — respond with your view
LongText: I would support a repair workshop, mainly because it would give students a chance to practise a skill that is easy to postpone learning. Maya is right that a film night could bring more people together, but attendance alone does not tell us how useful an activity would be. At a workshop, even a small group could learn how to replace a bicycle light or mend a torn pocket, then help friends with the same problem later. I also agree with Daniel that safety matters. The university could begin with simple repairs that do not involve electrical wiring, and invite trained volunteers to supervise. Students could bring an item in advance so organisers know which tools are needed. This would make the event manageable without removing its practical value. A film night could still be organised by existing clubs, while the repair workshop would offer something students are less likely to find elsewhere on campus.

Description: 自拟四级作文题 · 介绍一个有用的校园学习习惯，解释作用并说明如何坚持 · 短篇为节选，长篇为完整原创回答
DescriptionEn: Original prompt: describe a useful campus study habit, explain its benefits and how to maintain it
LongText: A useful habit I developed at university is writing a short plan before leaving the library. I do not list everything I hope to finish during the following week. Instead, I write down the first task I want to complete the next morning and the materials I will need. This small habit saves more time than I expected. Previously, I often spent the beginning of a study session choosing what to do. Now I can open the right book and start immediately. The plan also helps me notice missing materials before I go home, when there is still time to borrow a book or ask a classmate. Of course, a plan sometimes needs to change. An urgent assignment may appear, or a task may take longer than expected. I simply adjust the note. Its purpose is to make starting easier, not to fill every hour with work. For me, that is enough to make the habit worth keeping.

Description: 自拟六级作文题 · 论述怎样让学习反馈更有用，结合师生双方的行动展开 · 短篇为节选，长篇为完整原创回答
DescriptionEn: Original prompt: how can learning feedback become more useful? Discuss actions for teachers and students
LongText: Feedback is most useful when students can act on it before their next piece of work. A page covered in corrections may look thorough, yet it can leave the writer uncertain about what to change first. Effective feedback therefore requires selection as well as accuracy. Teachers can help by identifying one or two priorities and illustrating them with examples from the student's own work. If an essay makes claims without supporting evidence, correcting every minor spelling error will not address its central weakness. A brief comment showing where an example is needed may produce a more significant improvement. Students should also have a chance to revise part of the assignment, so they can test whether they have understood the advice. The student has responsibilities too. Reading a comment only to check the mark turns a learning opportunity into a record of past performance. Keeping a short list of recurring problems and reviewing it before the next assignment makes feedback easier to use. Good feedback does not need to solve every problem at once. It should help students recognise a specific weakness, make a practical change, and gradually become more capable of judging their own work.
ShortText: Feedback is most useful when students can act on it before their next piece of work. A page covered in corrections may look thorough, yet it can leave the writer uncertain about what to change first. Effective feedback therefore requires selection as well as accuracy.
Title: CET-6 · Feedback that students can use

LongText: The community centre keeps a spare key in a small green box behind the reception desk. When I arrived to open the room for our drawing class, the box was empty. I checked the booking sheet, called the previous group, and finally noticed a note beside the kettle. Someone had moved the key to a dry shelf after spilling a cup of tea. By then, three people were waiting outside the classroom. One had brought a bowl of lemons to draw, another carried an empty frame, and the third was still deciding whether she wanted to join. I unlocked the door and found that the morning light reached every table. We moved the lemons away from the heater and placed the frame against a blue wall. The new visitor borrowed a pencil and chose the chair nearest the window. At the end of the session, nobody had finished quite the picture they expected. The lemons appeared in several different sizes, and the frame had become part of a drawing instead of a place to put one. Before leaving, I dried the green box, put the key inside, and wrote a clearer note for the next person.

from collections import defaultdict
from decimal import Decimal


def summarize_purchases(rows):
    totals = defaultdict(lambda: Decimal("0.00"))
    counts = defaultdict(int)

    for category, price, quantity in rows:
        amount = Decimal(price) * quantity
        totals[category] += amount
        counts[category] += quantity

    report = []
    for category in sorted(totals):
        report.append({
            "category": category,
            "items": counts[category],
            "total": totals[category],
        })
    return report


def print_report(report):
    grand_total = Decimal("0.00")
    for item in report:
        line = "{category}: {items} items, {total:.2f}"
        print(line.format(**item))
        grand_total += item["total"]
    print("Grand total: {:.2f}".format(grand_total))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    purchases = [
        ("stationery", "2.40", 3),
        ("snacks", "1.75", 2),
        ("stationery", "4.10", 1),
    ]
    print_report(summarize_purchases(purchases))

WITH paid_totals AS (
    SELECT o.order_id,
           SUBSTR(o.placed_on, 1, 7) AS month,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS amount
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'paid'
    GROUP BY o.order_id, SUBSTR(o.placed_on, 1, 7)
)
SELECT month,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(amount), 2) AS average_order
FROM paid_totals
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;

Description: 洗碗时发现厨房时钟总是慢三分钟
DescriptionEn: A kitchen clock and a small household habit
LongText: The clock above our kitchen sink loses three minutes every week. My brother wants to replace it, but I have grown used to its small delay. On Tuesday evenings, while the dinner plates soak, I stand on a chair and move the hands forward. Then I wipe a circle of dust from the glass with my sleeve. Last week, my brother came home early and found me halfway through this routine. He held the chair steady while I reached for the clock. Behind its crooked frame lay a folded shopping receipt from the previous winter. We had bought oranges, soap, and a cake for our mother's birthday that day. He remembered carrying the cake home on a crowded bus. I remembered dropping one orange under a seat. Neither memory had occurred to us for months. We put the receipt in a drawer and returned the clock to its nail. My brother stopped suggesting a replacement. When dinner finished, he washed the plates while I dried them, both of us occasionally glancing at the unreliable hands.

Description: 晚归读者在还书口前遇见熟悉的书
DescriptionEn: A borrowed book finds its way back
LongText: I reached the library six minutes after closing, carrying a novel that was already overdue. The building was dark except for a lamp behind the information desk. Beside the entrance, a metal flap marked the return slot. I opened it, lowered the book into the narrow space, and heard a soft thump from the box below. Before I could leave, someone tapped on the glass. The librarian held up a knitted scarf. I had left it on a reading chair the previous Saturday. She came to the side door and passed it to me, wrapped around a small paperback. The paperback belonged to me too, although I had forgotten bringing it. I asked how she remembered whose things they were. She pointed to the blue thread that marked my place in both books. Apparently, I was the only regular reader who used a piece of yarn instead of a bookmark. Outside, the wind had sharpened. I wound the scarf around my neck and walked home with one less borrowed book and one more book than expected.

Description: 邻居借出的梯子连接了两个家庭的小事
DescriptionEn: Borrowing a ladder leads to a shared repair
LongText: Our hallway light failed on Saturday morning, and none of our chairs was tall enough to reach it safely. I knocked on the apartment opposite ours to borrow a ladder. Mr. Bell opened the door with flour on his shirt. He said the ladder was in his cupboard, behind three empty boxes and a folded camping table. We pulled everything into the hallway. While he searched for the ladder's rubber feet, I noticed that the cupboard door dragged across the floor. He had been meaning to fix it for months. After changing our bulb, I brought the ladder back with a screwdriver from my own kitchen drawer. The loose hinge needed only a little adjustment. Mr. Bell tested the door several times, pleased by its sudden silence. Then a timer rang inside his apartment. He returned with two warm rolls on a plate, explaining the flour on his shirt. We ate standing beside the camping table. By noon, our hallway was bright, his cupboard closed properly, and the ladder had finally found a place near the front.

Description: 一次突然降雨打乱了屋顶晾衣的安排
DescriptionEn: Neighbors rescue laundry before the rain
LongText: The apartment roof has six washing lines and a view of the railway. On clear mornings, sheets float above the chimneys while trains slide through the gap between two warehouses. I usually carry my laundry up before breakfast. That Thursday, every line was full except the shortest one, so I folded my large sheet over itself twice. At lunchtime, clouds arrived without the usual warning breeze. I was in a shop two streets away when the first drops struck the window. By the time I reached our building, water was pouring from the roof drain. I hurried upstairs, expecting to find everything soaked. My sheet was gone. In its place hung an empty row of wooden pegs. Downstairs, a note waited under my door: "Dry things in the basket by the lift." Someone had collected the laundry from all six lines and sorted it into neat piles. I recognized the basket from the apartment above mine. That evening, I returned it with the pegs in a paper bag and a fresh loaf tucked underneath.

Description: 一张共用购物清单让室友发现彼此的习惯
DescriptionEn: A shared shopping list becomes more precise
LongText: When Clara moved into our flat, we agreed to share groceries. A notebook lived beside the kettle, ready for anyone to add an item. During the first week, the system seemed perfect. Then I wrote "apples" on the list. Clara returned from the market with a bag of tiny sour ones, exactly the kind I never bought. She sliced one into thin pieces and sprinkled them over her lunch. I preferred large, sweet apples that could survive a day in my backpack. We discovered similar differences about bread, coffee, and the meaning of "a little cheese." Our simple list had hidden a surprising number of private instructions. Instead of giving up, we began adding details. Bread needed a note about slicing. Coffee received a brand name. Next to apples, we drew two small boxes, one for each of us. The notebook became untidy, full of arrows and jokes. Shopping took slightly longer, but we stopped bringing home food the other person would avoid. By winter, we could often fill the basket without opening the notebook at all.

Description: 失落的手套在公交站等待主人
DescriptionEn: A lost mitten draws quiet attention
LongText: A red mitten appeared on the fence beside our bus stop one cold morning. Someone had pushed its thumb between two bars so it would not fall. For three days, I passed it on my way to work. The wool grew stiff with frost, then softened in the afternoon sun. Nobody seemed to claim it. On Friday, a child's drawing was tied to the fence. It showed a pair of red hands waving above the words "Missing a friend?" The mitten remained beside it. A passenger waiting with me said she had seen the little boy who made the picture. His own mittens were green. The next Monday, both the drawing and the mitten had disappeared. A new paper hung in their place, protected inside a clear food bag. "Found, thank you," it said, with a photograph of two red mittens on a kitchen table. I read the message while my bus approached. The other passengers leaned closer, smiling at a story none of us had needed to tell aloud.

Description: 修补外套时翻出旧纽扣盒里的故事
DescriptionEn: A coat repair opens a tin of memories
LongText: My winter coat lost a button on the first truly cold day of the year. At home, I searched the drawer where useful things gradually become tangled. Beneath a spare cable and two blunt pencils sat my grandmother's button tin. Its lid showed a faded blue ship. Inside were dozens of buttons, all carefully saved from forgotten clothes. The coat needed a large brown button. I found five almost suitable ones and placed them on the table. One was too shiny. Another had a crack near its edge. As I compared them, I recognized the small white buttons from a childhood school shirt. A square green one belonged to a jacket my grandmother wore in the garden. Eventually, I chose a plain wooden button that matched nothing exactly. Sewing it on took ten minutes, including the time spent threading the needle twice. The result sat slightly lower than its neighbors, but the coat closed properly. I returned every unused button to the tin and added the loose button from a shirt I no longer wore.

Description: 重新摆放一把椅子改变了周末的阅读习惯
DescriptionEn: A room changes when one chair moves
LongText: For two years, my reading chair faced a blank wall. It was the only place it seemed to fit between the bookcase and the door. On a rainy Sunday, I moved it beside the window while cleaning. From there, I could see a narrow strip of garden and the top of a neighbor's yellow shed. I sat down to test the view and stayed for an hour. Rain tapped the window at different speeds. A cat crossed the wall, paused beneath the shed roof, and vanished. The book in my lap remained unopened, yet the hour did not feel wasted. Later, I tried rearranging the rest of the room around the chair. That produced a blocked cupboard and a lamp cable stretched across the floor. I put everything else back and left only the chair in its new place. Now I carry a small table over when I want tea. Visitors sometimes ask why the furniture looks slightly uneven. I point to the window, where there is usually something ordinary worth watching for a minute.

Description: 电梯里的一张告示帮助新住户搬家
DescriptionEn: An elevator notice makes moving day easier
LongText: The note in our lift was written on the back of a cereal box. "Moving into number twelve on Saturday. Sorry about the boxes," it said. Below the words was a drawing of an exhausted person carrying a sofa. I read it twice during the slow journey to my floor, mostly because the sofa looked larger than the person. Saturday arrived with steady rain. At the entrance, two newcomers were struggling to keep cardboard boxes dry while their van occupied the loading space. I held the door as they carried the first pile inside. A neighbor from the ground floor appeared with an old towel for the lift floor. Soon, the move had acquired a small team. One person guarded the entrance, another stacked empty boxes, and a teenager carried houseplants upstairs. The sofa barely fitted around the final corner. By afternoon, a second note replaced the first. It invited anyone who had helped to number twelve for tea. The drawing now showed the same exhausted person asleep comfortably on the sofa.

Description: 清晨候车时观察一座尚未苏醒的车站
DescriptionEn: Waiting for an early train
LongText: At half past five, the station clock seemed brighter than the sky. I had arrived much too early for my train because the guesthouse owner had warned me about traffic. There was none. The ticket hall smelled of floor cleaner, and a man in an orange jacket was pushing a machine slowly around the empty benches. A bakery shutter rose at six. The woman behind the counter sold me a warm roll and pointed toward the platform door. She said it would open soon, although the train would not leave for another forty minutes. I ate beside a window while the first commuters arrived, carrying the calm expressions of people who knew exactly where to stand. When the platform finally opened, I followed them through the door. Beyond the roof, the sky had turned pale pink. A cleaner waved to the train driver, who returned the gesture from the cab. My long wait had shown me the station assembling itself for the day. I found my seat, placed my bag overhead, and watched the familiar bakery window move out of sight.

Description: 渡轮上的雨天旅程带来意外的海岸风景
DescriptionEn: A rainy crossing to an island
LongText: Rain covered the ferry windows before we left the harbor. I had imagined standing on the deck, taking photographs of the island as it approached. Instead, I sat beside a cloudy pane with my coat folded on my knees. Across the aisle, a woman balanced three paper cups and a bag of bread for her family. She offered me the spare cup when she noticed that the cafe had closed for the crossing. It contained tea, already sweetened. We talked about the island road, where she said sheep sometimes gathered near the sharpest bend. Her children counted fishing boats until the shore disappeared behind the weather. Halfway across, the rain eased. A crew member opened the deck door, and several of us stepped outside. The island appeared gradually, first as a gray shape, then as fields, roofs, and a white wall above the landing. My photographs showed mostly wet railings. I kept them anyway. At the harbor, the family waved and hurried toward a waiting car. I followed the narrow road uphill, watching carefully for sheep at every bend.

Description: 一把系着木鱼的钥匙带来安静的住宿体验
DescriptionEn: Arriving at a small guesthouse
LongText: The guesthouse key hung from a wooden fish nearly as long as my hand. Its owner explained that guests had once lost too many plain keys. Nobody could forget this one in a pocket without noticing it. She gave me directions to my room, then drew a small map showing the path to the nearest place serving dinner. My room faced a courtyard containing two bicycles and a lemon tree in a cracked pot. I left the window open while unpacking. Below, someone washed dishes, and a radio played quietly behind a door. After a day of unfamiliar streets, those domestic sounds were unexpectedly reassuring. I followed the map to a family cafe where the owner recognized the wooden fish immediately. Apparently, guests had been bringing it there for years. He asked which room I occupied and recommended the vegetable soup. When I returned, the courtyard lights were on. I placed the key on the bedside table, where its large painted eye watched over my guidebook until morning.

Description: 旅行结束前寄出一张写得很慢的明信片
DescriptionEn: Finding words for a final postcard
LongText: On the last afternoon of my trip, I bought a postcard showing the harbor at sunset. The harbor outside the shop was bright with midday light and smelled strongly of fuel. I sat at a cafe to write to my father. After his address, I could think of nothing more interesting than a list of places I had visited. The waiter brought water and moved the postcard away from a damp circle on the table. At the next table, two brothers argued over a folded map. A delivery rider stopped to ask directions. Somewhere behind the kitchen, a plate broke, followed by a burst of laughter. I began writing about those small interruptions. I mentioned the cafe's chipped green cups and the dog sleeping beneath my chair. By the time the message reached the edge, I had said almost nothing about the famous buildings. The post office was three streets away. I dropped the card into its box and walked back through the harbor, hoping my father would recognize the kind of afternoon I had enjoyed.

Description: 步行路线临时改道，经过一片正在收果的果园
DescriptionEn: A closed path leads through an orchard
LongText: A handwritten sign blocked the footpath just beyond the village. A fallen tree had damaged a small bridge, and walkers were directed along an orchard track instead. My printed map showed only a dotted line there. I checked the sign twice, tightened the straps on my bag, and followed a series of yellow arrows tied to fence posts. The track passed between apple trees supported by rough wooden poles. Workers were lifting fruit into shallow crates. One woman called out to ask whether the arrows were easy to see. She had put them up before breakfast because several visitors had reached the damaged bridge the previous day. I told her they were clear and asked how far the detour continued. She pointed to a barn at the top of the field. Beyond it, the original path crossed open grass toward the hills. Before I left, she placed two small apples in my hand. I ate one by the barn and saved the other for lunch. The extra walk added nearly an hour, but I stopped checking the map so often afterward.

Description: 破损的行李箱轮子让一次转乘变得格外难忘
DescriptionEn: Managing a broken suitcase wheel
LongText: My suitcase began making a knocking sound outside the hotel. By the next corner, one wheel had stopped turning completely. The station was only fifteen minutes away, but the streets were paved with uneven stones. Each time I pulled the handle, the case bounced behind me like an angry animal determined to attract everyone's attention. I tried carrying it and discovered how many books I had bought during the week. A shopkeeper watched my struggle, then came outside with a length of packing cord. Together, we tied the loose wheel against the case so it could not swing. That stopped the knocking, although I still had to drag the suitcase at an awkward angle. At the station, I arrived tired, warm, and just early enough. I sat on my case while waiting for the platform number. A traveler beside me admired the cord and said it looked like a sailing knot. I admitted that I had no idea what it was called. It held until I reached home, where I finally unpacked the books before doing anything else.

Description: 露营地的一盏灯让陌生旅人开始交谈
DescriptionEn: A shared lamp at a quiet campsite
LongText: We reached the campsite after the small office had closed. A board listed empty pitches, and an envelope held instructions for late arrivals. Our assigned space stood beneath a broad tree, beside a tent whose owners were already asleep. We put up our shelter by torchlight, whispering whenever a metal pole fell against another pole. In the morning, our neighbors apologized for sleeping through the noise. They offered coffee while we struggled to light our stove. We exchanged advice about the walking routes and discovered that all four of us had packed too much food. By evening, our separate meals had become one large, improvised dinner. The campsite had few lights, so we placed our camping lamp on an overturned bucket between the tents. It illuminated a circle of grass, four bowls, and the steam rising from a saucepan. Beyond that circle, the field disappeared into darkness. We stayed talking until moths began landing on the empty plates. Before bed, someone moved the lamp closer to the path for the next late arrivals.

Our assigned space stood beneath a broad tree, beside a tent whose owners were already asleep. We put up our shelter by torchlight, whispering whenever a metal pole fell against another pole.
Title: A Lamp Between Tents

Description: 坐到终点站后发现一处平常而安静的海滨
DescriptionEn: Riding a tram beyond the tourist center
LongText: I boarded the tram intending to travel only three stops. Then a seat opened beside the window, and I decided to remain until the end of the line. The busy shopping streets gave way to apartment blocks, small workshops, and gardens. A woman carrying a folded ironing board got off beside a shop selling bicycle parts. At the final stop, the driver pointed toward the return platform. I thanked him but walked instead toward a patch of blue visible between two buildings. Five minutes later, I reached a promenade. There were no souvenir stalls, only a closed snack kiosk and several benches facing the water. An elderly man was repairing a fishing line on one bench. Farther along, two children pushed a toy truck through the sand. I sat with the lunch I had bought downtown and watched a gull investigate the empty kiosk. After an hour, I took the tram back. The famous square was crowded when I returned, but the quiet end of the line remained the clearest part of my day.

Description: 窗外树枝上的鸟巢让办公室有了新话题
DescriptionEn: Watching a nest from an office window
LongText: From my desk, I could see a fork in the tree outside the office window. In early spring, a bird began bringing thin twigs to it. Most mornings, I arrived to find the little structure slightly larger. My colleague lowered the blind halfway so we could watch without standing directly against the glass and disturbing its builder. For a while, the bird seemed to spend more time correcting mistakes than adding new material. A long piece of grass dangled from the side for three days. Then the visits became less frequent, and we wondered whether the nest had been abandoned. One afternoon, a movement inside answered our question. We never had a perfect view of the young birds. Their heads appeared briefly above the rim, then vanished. Weeks later, the nest was empty. The branch looked oddly plain without its constant traffic. When autumn removed the leaves, we could finally see how firmly the nest sat between the branches. Nobody suggested taking it down. In winter, it caught a small cap of snow that remained after the surrounding twigs were bare.

Title: A Nest Beyond the Window

Description: 在池塘边安静等待，发现水面的细小变化
DescriptionEn: An early visit to a neighborhood pond
LongText: The pond looked empty when I arrived before breakfast. A pale mist covered the far bank, hiding the fence and the lower branches of the willows. I sat on a wooden platform with my flask between my shoes. At first, the only movement came from drops falling off the reeds and making small circles on the water. After ten minutes, details began to separate from the gray. A dark bird stood so still on the opposite bank that I had mistaken it for a broken stump. Something small moved through the reeds near my feet. A fish touched the surface, leaving a widening ring that reached the platform. By the time a dog walker appeared on the path, the mist had lifted enough to reveal the whole pond. She asked whether I had seen anything interesting. I described the bird, the rings, and the moving reeds. She nodded and said she came here every morning but rarely stopped. We watched together for another minute, until her dog sat down with a heavy sigh and reminded us both of breakfast.

Title: Morning at the Pond

Description: 风后的一根断枝呈现树木不易察觉的细节
DescriptionEn: Examining a branch after a storm
LongText: After the wind died, a thick branch lay across the garden path. It had fallen from the old tree near the gate, scattering wet leaves over the paving stones. My first thought was that clearing it would spoil the morning. I fetched gloves and a saw, then stopped beside the broken end to look more closely. The wood was lighter inside than I expected. Along the bark ran tiny ridges, pale patches, and a narrow line where another branch had once grown. A strip of moss held enough water to darken my glove. Up in the tree, all these details had been too high to see. I cut the branch into manageable pieces and carried them behind the shed. The smaller twigs went into a loose pile near the hedge. By lunchtime, the path was clear. Over the following weeks, the cut wood gradually lost its sharp, fresh smell. The tree's missing branch left a gap through which afternoon light reached a corner of the garden that had always been shaded before.

Title: The Fallen Branch

Description: 退潮后的岩石水洼映出一个微小世界
DescriptionEn: Looking closely at a coastal rock pool
LongText: We reached the rocks when the water had drawn back from the shore. My cousin hurried toward the largest pool, but I stopped at a shallow one beside my shoe. It was no wider than a dinner plate. A strand of green weed crossed its center, and the sky reflected so clearly that the bottom was difficult to see. When I moved my shadow over the water, the reflection faded. Small shells clung to the sides. A creature no longer than my thumbnail slipped beneath a stone. Sand shifted at the bottom, although I could not tell what had disturbed it. I called my cousin back, and we crouched beside the pool without touching anything. For several minutes, the little space seemed busier than the open beach. Then a larger wave reached the outer rocks, reminding us that the tide would return. We stepped back along the dry route we had used before. From the path above, our pool disappeared among hundreds of dark hollows, each waiting to become part of the sea again.

Description: 雨后花园里的蜗牛迫使园丁放慢脚步
DescriptionEn: A garden path becomes a snail crossing
LongText: Rain ended just before sunset, leaving the garden path dark and shiny. I went outside to collect a forgotten trowel and nearly stepped on a snail. Then I noticed another by the drain and three more near the pots. Their shells looked polished in the low light. I set the trowel down and waited for the nearest one to move. It advanced across a narrow crack, extending itself cautiously before pulling its shell forward. A second snail followed a line that appeared to lead straight toward the first, but they passed without meeting. I could see thin trails behind them when I bent close to the paving. The watering can stood at the far end of the path, surrounded by fresh travelers from the border. Reaching it now required an absurdly careful series of steps. I decided the forgotten tools could stay outside until morning. From the kitchen doorway, I watched the path for a little longer. Darkness gradually hid the shells, but the silver trails remained visible wherever the last light touched them.

Description: 熟悉的小山在雾中显得陌生而安静
DescriptionEn: Walking a familiar hill in low cloud
LongText: I know the hill above our town well enough to recognize its turns by the stones underfoot. In fog, that confidence became less useful. The path ahead faded after a few steps, and the town below was entirely hidden. I kept to the marked route, listening to my boots and the occasional drip from the wire fence. Without the wide view, nearby things claimed my attention. Water hung along a spider's web stretched between two dry stalks. A sheep appeared beside the path like a pale rock, then turned its head. The wooden gate, usually visible from far away, arrived suddenly out of the gray. At the shelter near the top, I drank tea and waited. For a moment, the fog thinned, revealing one red roof far below. Then it closed again. I began the return walk before the afternoon grew late. Halfway down, the cloud lifted enough to show the whole valley. The hill had not changed, but I had finally noticed several things I normally passed while looking toward the horizon.

Title: The Hill in Fog

Description: 新雪上的足迹记录了看不见的清晨活动
DescriptionEn: Following tracks in fresh snow
LongText: Snow fell during the night, covering the garden with an even white layer. From the back door, I could see several lines of footprints crossing it. One began beneath the hedge and ended near the bird feeder. Another followed the wall before turning sharply around a flowerpot. I put on boots, careful to leave the clearest tracks untouched. Some prints were easy to recognize. Our neighbor's cat had left a tidy row beside the wall. Smaller marks near the feeder were surrounded by scattered seed. Farther away, a set of tracks confused me because the gaps between them changed so much. I followed them only with my eyes, unwilling to cover the pattern with my own steps. By noon, the sun softened every edge. A lump of snow dropped from the feeder, wiping out part of the busiest crossing. I took one photograph before going inside. The next morning, almost all the snow had gone. The garden looked quiet again, although its visitors had probably followed exactly the same routes while I slept.

Title: Footprints Across the Snow

Description: 观察庭院树木一整年带来的细小发现
DescriptionEn: A year's observations of one courtyard tree
LongText: The tree in our courtyard has no sign identifying it. I used to pass beneath it without wondering what kind it was. Then a neighbor began photographing the same branch every Sunday. She showed me the pictures on her phone: bare twigs, tight buds, young leaves, and finally a thick green screen hiding the windows behind it. I started keeping my own smaller record. On a calendar, I noted the first fallen leaf I found, the morning birds gathered after rain, and the week the shade reached our kitchen door. These were rough observations, often interrupted by travel or forgetfulness. Still, they made the seasons feel less like sudden changes. In autumn, the courtyard cleaner piled the leaves near the gate. I helped fill two sacks and discovered how many colors existed inside what I had called a brown pile. When winter came, the branch in my neighbor's photographs was bare again. We compared our records over coffee. Her pictures were orderly; my calendar was crowded with uncertain dates. Both gave the tree a history we could recognize.

Title: The Courtyard Tree

Description: 学生用纸桥承重实验比较不同折法
DescriptionEn: A classroom compares folded paper bridges
LongText: Ms. Patel gave each group one sheet of paper, two books, and a handful of coins. The task was to build a bridge across the gap between the books. Leo laid his paper flat. It held three coins before bending deeply in the middle. Across the table, Mina folded her sheet into a row of narrow ridges. Her bridge carried far more coins, but the class soon discovered a problem with their comparison. The gaps were different widths, and some groups had stacked coins in one place while others spread them out. They agreed on a gap, a coin size, and a rule for adding weight. During the second round, Leo carefully copied Mina's folds. His bridge lasted longer than his first one, though not as long as hers. A crooked fold seemed to explain the difference. He wrote down the result instead of hiding it. Before the bell, each group drew its bridge and listed what had stayed the same during the test. Several students asked to take fresh paper home. The coins, Ms. Patel said, had to remain in the classroom jar.

Title: The Paper Bridge Test

Description: 用三个杯子比较不同条件下茶水变凉的速度
DescriptionEn: Comparing how three cups cool
LongText: Nora's tea always became cold while she answered messages. One Saturday, she decided to watch the cooling instead of complaining about it. She poured equal amounts of hot tea into three matching mugs. One stayed uncovered, one received a small plate as a lid, and the third stood inside a folded towel on the kitchen table. Every five minutes, she checked each cup with the same thermometer and wrote the readings in a notebook. Moving the lid and thermometer took longer than expected. She also noticed that the towel prevented her from holding the mug in the usual way, so she left all three handles alone. The cups did not cool at the same rate. Nora resisted making a grand conclusion from one untidy morning experiment. The next day, she repeated it, changing the order in which she measured the cups. Her notes became stained with tea, but the pattern was clearer. By Monday, a small plate had earned a permanent place beside her usual mug. Answering messages still took too long, though her drink now stayed pleasant longer.

Title: Three Cups of Tea

Description: 空走廊和铺了地毯的房间有不同声音
DescriptionEn: Listening to sound in different spaces
LongText: The school hallway sounded enormous after everyone had gone home. Ben clapped once beside the lockers and heard the sound linger. In the nearby music room, the same clap seemed much shorter. He brought his friend over to listen. They repeated the test several times, becoming quieter whenever they remembered that the caretaker was working downstairs. The rooms differed in more than size. The hallway had a hard floor and long bare walls. The music room contained curtains, padded chairs, and a large rug. Their teacher suggested recording a few simple sounds from the same distance rather than trusting memory alone. They used a phone to record claps and a spoken sentence in both places. Back in class, their friends could identify most of the recordings without seeing the rooms. A final recording confused everyone: it came from the hallway while a group of students stood along the walls. Ben added that detail to his notes. The spaces had taught him to ask who and what were inside a room before describing how it sounded.

Description: 同一根木杆的影子在一天里改变位置
DescriptionEn: Tracking a stick's changing shadow
LongText: A wooden stick stood upright in a bucket of sand beside the classroom door. At nine o'clock, the class marked the end of its shadow with chalk. They returned before lunch and found that the shadow had moved away from the first mark. A student drew a second cross, adding the time in careful blue numbers. The children expected the next mark to continue in a straight line from the others. Their afternoon observations challenged that prediction. Some shadows were shorter, and the direction changed as well. Clouds interrupted two visits, leaving gaps in the record that no amount of patient staring could fill. At the end of the day, they connected their observations on a large sheet of paper. The teacher asked which statements came directly from the marks and which were explanations they had added. The distinction prompted an unexpectedly long discussion. They left the bucket in place for another clear day. Meanwhile, the caretaker asked them to move the chalk crosses away from the main walking route, where several visitors had stopped to wonder about the mysterious blue trail.

Title: A Shadow on the Playground

Description: 种子观察记录提醒学生重视清楚的标签
DescriptionEn: A seed experiment depends on careful labels
LongText: Three bean seeds sat on damp paper in a clear container. Three more rested in dry paper beside them. Ava placed both containers on the same shelf and wrote the date in her notebook. She wanted to compare what happened over the following week. Her younger brother wanted to know whether they would grow quickly enough to watch during breakfast. For two days, little seemed to change. Ava checked the paper each morning, adding a small amount of water only to the damp container. On the third day, she noticed a pale point emerging from one seed. She drew it larger than life in the notebook so she could include its shape. Then she discovered that both containers had identical lids and no labels. Fortunately, the paper still made their conditions obvious, but the mistake bothered her. She added labels to the bases and recorded exactly what she had done. By the end of the week, her brother had lost interest in watching breakfast miracles. Ava, however, had learned to find small daily changes more satisfying than the dramatic beginning she had expected.

Description: 做饼干时学习厨房秤上归零按钮的用途
DescriptionEn: A baking lesson with a kitchen scale
LongText: Sam wanted to make biscuits without asking for help. The recipe called for flour by weight, so he placed a bowl on the kitchen scale and began pouring. The number rose faster than he expected. When his sister arrived, the bowl contained only a small hill of flour, although the display already showed the amount in the recipe. She asked what the empty bowl had weighed. Sam had not checked. They transferred the flour to another container, weighed the bowl, and discovered where much of the total had come from. Then she showed him the button that reset the reading with the bowl still in place. Sam began again, adding flour slowly near the target amount. He kept a spoon nearby to remove the final excess. The biscuits were unevenly shaped, and two became darker than the rest, but the dough had the right texture. While they cooled, he wrote a note beside the recipe: "Bowl first. Zero. Flour." Next time, he planned to work on making every biscuit roughly the same size.

Description: 用气球和纸屑探索摩擦后的细小现象
DescriptionEn: Testing what a rubbed balloon can attract
LongText: At the kitchen table, Priya cut a scrap of paper into tiny squares. Her father inflated a balloon and rubbed it against his wool sleeve. When he held it near the pieces, several jumped upward and clung to the surface. Priya laughed, then asked why the demonstration had failed when she tried it at a friend's house. They decided to compare materials without changing everything at once. First, they used the same balloon and paper but rubbed against a cotton cloth. Then they tried the sleeve again. Priya counted the pieces that lifted and wrote rough results on the back of the remaining scrap. The numbers varied more than she expected. Sometimes paper touched the balloon and sometimes it did not. Her father suggested noting the distance and how long they rubbed, rather than declaring one material the winner immediately. By the end, the table was covered in tiny squares. Priya used the balloon to collect a few, but most required an ordinary brush. The cleanup gave her another result to record: interesting experiments could still create a very familiar mess.

Description: 透过彩色薄膜观察物品颜色的变化
DescriptionEn: Looking at familiar objects through colored film
LongText: The art room received a box of colored transparent film. Instead of cutting it immediately, Daniel held a red sheet in front of his eyes. The room changed at once. A blue folder looked strangely dark, while a red pencil seemed less different from its surroundings. He called his partner over and asked her to describe what she saw. They arranged colored pencils, white paper, and a green leaf on a desk. Taking turns, they looked through different sheets and recorded which objects appeared bright or dark. Their descriptions did not always match, partly because one student stood nearer the window. They moved their chairs together and compared again. The activity began as preparation for a collage, but it became a lesson in looking carefully. Daniel realized that naming an object's ordinary color did not fully describe its appearance through a filter. For the finished artwork, he built a small cardboard frame holding three colored panels. Classmates could slide it across the pencil arrangement and see the changes themselves, adding observations on sticky notes around the edge.

Description: 从面包店后门看见城市清晨的准备工作
DescriptionEn: A city block wakes around a bakery
LongText: At five in the morning, the bakery's front window was dark, but its back door stood open. Warm air drifted into the lane, carrying the smell of bread. A delivery driver rolled empty trays toward his van. Above him, someone shook a blanket from a bedroom window, then quickly pulled it inside when the baker looked up. The lane served several businesses, and each seemed to begin its day at a different hour. The newspaper shop received a bundle wrapped in blue plastic. A cafe owner unlocked her shutters while talking into a phone. Two street cleaners paused beside the bakery door, where the baker handed them small paper bags. By seven, the front street looked ready for customers. The lane became quiet, its bins lined neatly against the walls. People approaching the bakery saw polished glass, bright shelves, and a tray of rolls near the till. From the corner, the delivery driver watched the first customer enter. Then he shut the van doors and drove away, leaving behind a block whose busy preparations were already difficult to imagine.

Description: 广场长椅一天中迎来不同的使用者
DescriptionEn: One public bench changes company
LongText: The bench beside the square faces away from the fountain. Visitors often ignore it because the view is mostly a bus shelter and a row of shops. At noon, however, it becomes the best seat in the area. The plane tree shades it completely, while the benches facing the fountain remain exposed to the strongest sun. A tailor from the corner shop usually eats there first. She leaves at twelve thirty, just before two office workers arrive with sandwiches. Later, a man with a shopping trolley rests while waiting for a bus. People sometimes speak, but often they simply share the shade with a polite space between them. During road repairs, workers placed a temporary fence around the tree and bench. For two weeks, its regular users stood elsewhere or walked farther into the square. When the fence came down, somebody tied a ribbon around one wooden arm. The tailor removed it before sitting down, folded it carefully, and put it in her pocket. By lunchtime, the bench had resumed its ordinary, useful life.

Description: 喷泉维修后重新成为街角的集合地点
DescriptionEn: A repaired fountain changes a small corner
LongText: For most of the summer, the fountain at the corner stood empty. Leaves gathered in its shallow basin, and a faded sign promised repairs. People began using its edge as a place to put shopping bags while checking their phones. Without the sound of water, traffic from the larger road seemed much closer than it had before. One Tuesday, two workers arrived with tools and a length of hose. They lifted a square panel from the pavement and spent hours kneeling beside it. A shopkeeper brought chairs for their lunch break. Children on their way home from school asked repeatedly whether the fountain would work that day. It did, shortly after four. The first burst splashed unevenly, then settled into a steady pattern. Several people stopped, watching as if the water were performing a difficult trick. The workers tested the controls and replaced the panel. By evening, the corner had recovered its softer background sound. Shopping bags moved to the nearby bench, and a little girl persuaded her father to walk around the block once more before going home.

Title: Water Returns to the Fountain

Description: 收摊后的市场展示城市日常工作的另一面
DescriptionEn: The last hour of a street market
LongText: At four o'clock, the market begins to change shape. Shoppers still move between the stalls, but empty crates appear beneath the tables. A fruit seller lowers the price of bruised peaches. Across the lane, a man packs socks into plastic boxes, keeping every pair together with quick, practiced movements that never seem to pause for conversation. The fish stall closes first. Its owner washes the counter and pulls a hose across the wet stones. Flower sellers wrap the remaining bunches in large sheets of paper. A cafe worker collects cups from the narrow shelf where stallholders leave them during the day. Each business has a private order for finishing. By five, the wide umbrellas are folded. Vans enter the spaces that shoppers occupied an hour earlier. What looked like a permanent arrangement becomes a bare street marked by damp rectangles and a few loose petals. A cleaner begins at the far end, working toward the square. Tomorrow, the stalls will rise before many windows open. For now, the street belongs to footsteps, delivery doors, and the sound of a brush crossing stone.

Title: When the Market Closes

Description: 一座狭窄的人行桥如何组织日常通行
DescriptionEn: Sharing a narrow bridge over a canal
LongText: The footbridge over the canal is barely wide enough for two bicycles to pass. Every morning, commuters cross it in both directions, adjusting their speed without discussion. Near the middle, the boards make a hollow sound beneath each wheel. Pedestrians often step aside at the widest section, looking down at the water while the busiest group rolls past. One winter morning, a repair crew closed half the bridge. Everyone had to take turns using a narrow strip along one side. At first, people hesitated, uncertain who should move first. Then a woman at the front raised her hand, letting the opposite group through. Others copied her gesture. The arrangement lasted three days. Nobody had officially organized it, and no sign explained the rules. By the final afternoon, regular users recognized one another well enough to exchange a brief smile. When the full bridge reopened, the stream of bicycles returned to its familiar rhythm. A few riders still lifted a hand near the middle, though there was once again room to pass without stopping.

Title: The Canal Footbridge

Description: 公交站的新地图帮助人们重新认识周边街区
DescriptionEn: An updated neighborhood map draws attention
LongText: Workers replaced the faded map at our bus shelter with a larger one. It showed side streets that had never fitted on the old version, along with tiny symbols for gardens, toilets, and walking paths. During the morning rush, people stood unusually close to the glass. Several buses arrived while passengers were still tracing routes with their fingers. A woman pointed out a path behind the sports hall. It connected two streets that I had always reached by making a long loop. Another passenger noticed that the map still used an old name for the community center. We compared what we knew, turning a normal wait into a discussion of the surrounding blocks. That evening, I tried the path behind the hall. It passed a small playground and emerged beside a wall covered in ivy. The shortcut saved only a few minutes, but it changed the shape of the neighborhood in my mind. The next morning, I arrived at the shelter early enough to look for another unfamiliar line beneath the glass.

Title: A Map Under the Glass

Description: 居民一起在小巷的灰墙上绘制壁画
DescriptionEn: A neighborhood paints a shared alley mural
LongText: The wall behind the shops had been painted gray so many times that old patches showed through in different shades. When the shopkeepers proposed a mural, everyone seemed to imagine something different. One wanted flowers, another wanted local buildings, and the owner of the repair shop suggested a giant bicycle with wheels stretching almost to the roof. The artist held a meeting in the alley with paper and colored pencils. Instead of choosing one idea, she asked people to draw objects they saw there every day. The drawings included crates, pigeons, delivery carts, umbrellas, and the repair shop's crooked blue sign. Over two weekends, volunteers helped fill the outlines. Younger children painted the lower stones while adults reached the upper sections from a safe platform. The finished wall showed an exaggerated version of the alley itself, lively and crowded with familiar details. Deliveries still blocked it every morning. Bins still stood beneath the painted pigeons. But people now paused before turning the corner, sometimes searching for the small object they had drawn on the artist's paper.
ShortText: The wall behind the shops had been painted gray so many times that old patches showed through in different shades. When the shopkeepers proposed a mural, everyone seemed to imagine something different. One wanted flowers, another wanted local buildings, and the owner of the repair shop suggested a giant bicycle with wheels stretching almost to the roof.
Title: Painting the Narrow Wall

Description: 深夜路口的交通灯陪伴最后一批行人
DescriptionEn: A city crossing near midnight
LongText: Near midnight, the crossing outside the cinema becomes quiet. The last audience leaves in small groups, discussing endings as they pull on coats. Across the road, a cleaner stacks chairs inside a restaurant. The pedestrian signal continues its patient cycle, turning green for an empty pavement, then red while no vehicle approaches from either direction at all. A cyclist stops beside the button, holding a bunch of flowers against the handlebar. A hospital worker arrives carrying shoes in a bag. For a few seconds, they wait together under the cinema's remaining light. Then a taxi passes, its roof sign reflected in the wet road. When the signal changes, both cross toward the bus stop. The cinema manager locks the doors and tests each handle before walking away. Inside the restaurant, the cleaner switches off the last light. The corner does not become completely silent; a bus will arrive soon, and someone is still unloading a van farther down the street. Yet the space between sounds has grown wide enough to hear footsteps from the opposite pavement.
ShortText: Near midnight, the crossing outside the cinema becomes quiet. The last audience leaves in small groups, discussing endings as they pull on coats. Across the road, a cleaner stacks chairs inside a restaurant. The pedestrian signal continues its patient cycle, turning green for an empty pavement, then red while no vehicle approaches from either direction at all.
Title: At the Late Crossing

Description: 修表师傅在午休前认真完成最后一件小事
DescriptionEn: A watch repairer finishes one small job
LongText: At twelve thirty, Mr. Lin turns the sign in his watch shop to "Closed." He does this even if he is still working. Otherwise, he says, lunch will keep moving farther into the afternoon until it meets dinner. On Wednesday, I arrived with a broken watch strap just as his hand reached for the sign by the door. He looked at the strap, then at the clock above his workbench. The repair needed a small pin, which he found in a drawer divided into dozens of narrow compartments. Through a magnifying lens, the tiny part appeared large enough to examine comfortably. Without it, I could barely see what he held. The work took less than five minutes. While I paid, he placed his tools in a precise row and covered the open watch on his desk. I asked whether he liked owning so many clocks. He smiled and said he mostly liked making things useful again. Then he picked up a lunchbox from beneath the counter and followed me out, locking the door firmly behind us.
ShortText: At twelve thirty, Mr. Lin turns the sign in his watch shop to "Closed." He does this even if he is still working. Otherwise, he says, lunch will keep moving farther into the afternoon until it meets dinner. On Wednesday, I arrived with a broken watch strap just as his hand reached for the sign by the door.
Title: The Watch Repairer's Lunch

Description: 学校路口的值守者记得孩子们不同的步调
DescriptionEn: A crossing guard knows the morning crowd
LongText: Every school morning, Mrs. Evans stands at the crossing in a bright coat. She knows which children will arrive early, which parents hurry, and which dog refuses to move until everyone has crossed. She does not know every name, although people assume she does. Sometimes, she remembers a red backpack or a pair of noisy wheels instead. When a new family moved into the neighborhood, their youngest child stopped at the curb several steps behind his brother. The traffic noise worried him. Mrs. Evans waited, lowered her free hand, and explained exactly when they would move. She used the same words each morning for the rest of the week. By Friday, the boy reached the curb beside his brother. He still watched her carefully, but he stepped forward as soon as she gave the signal. That afternoon, he presented her with a drawing of the crossing. She was the largest figure on the page, taller than the buses. She folded it into her coat pocket and stayed at her post until the last family had passed.

She knows which children will arrive early, which parents hurry, and which dog refuses to move until everyone has crossed. She does not know every name, although people assume she does. Sometimes, she remembers a red backpack or a pair of noisy wheels instead.
Title: The Crossing Guard's Names

Description: 合唱团新成员慢慢找到自己的声音
DescriptionEn: A new singer learns to join a choir
LongText: On his first evening with the community choir, Martin chose a chair near the back. He had sung at home for years but had never followed printed music with other people. The page looked crowded with marks. When the conductor lifted her hands, he opened his mouth a moment late and quickly lost track of the line. The singer beside him pointed to the right place without interrupting her own part. During the break, she showed him where to mark his breathing and how to follow the repeated section. Martin apologized for singing too softly. She said hearing the people around him was a useful place to begin. Over the following weeks, he learned the shape of the rehearsals. Difficult passages returned often. Mistakes sometimes produced laughter, especially when everyone made the same one. At the winter concert, Martin still kept one finger near the lines he found tricky. Yet he no longer waited for his neighbor before beginning. When their section entered, his voice arrived with the others, steady enough for him to hear it clearly.

The page looked crowded with marks. When the conductor lifted her hands, he opened his mouth a moment late and quickly lost track of the line.
Title: A Place in the Choir

Description: 退休后的祖父认真学习成为一名园艺新手
DescriptionEn: An experienced adult becomes a beginner
LongText: After retiring, my grandfather rented a small vegetable plot. Everyone expected him to know what to do because he had spent years repairing engines and building furniture. He knew almost nothing about growing food. On his first visit, he carried a new notebook, two borrowed tools, and a packet of seeds whose instructions he read several times. The gardener in the next plot was younger than his youngest daughter. She showed him how to mark rows with string and leave room between plants. He listened without pretending that the advice was obvious. At home, he drew a plan and wrote questions in the margin. His first harvest filled only a small bowl. Some plants had grown poorly, and he had pulled up something useful while removing weeds. Still, he brought the bowl to Sunday lunch and explained every mistake with cheerful precision. The following spring, his notebook contained muddy fingerprints and many crossed-out plans. When I asked whether gardening was harder than fixing engines, he said engines usually stayed where you put them. Then he returned to measuring his rows.

He knew almost nothing about growing food. On his first visit, he carried a new notebook, two borrowed tools, and a packet of seeds whose instructions he read several times.
Title: Grandfather's New Notebook

Description: 送货员用熟悉的小细节辨认一条日常路线
DescriptionEn: A courier remembers a route through people
LongText: Lena delivers parcels along the same route most afternoons. She knows the buildings by their entrances more than their street numbers. One has a heavy door that sticks after rain. Another has a bell so quiet that she must wait beside it. At the end of the route, a retired teacher always asks whether she has eaten lunch. During a week of roadworks, Lena had to approach the neighborhood from the opposite direction. The familiar buildings appeared in a different order. She passed one entrance before recognizing its blue step, then walked back with a parcel tucked under her arm. Her carefully learned route suddenly required thought again. By Thursday, she had adjusted. She discovered a public tap near the park and a covered place to sort small packages when it rained. The teacher at the final stop noticed that she arrived later than usual. Lena explained the diversion, and they spent a minute comparing the old and new roads. Before she left, he handed her a pear in a paper bag. She ate it while walking to the van.
